title: Murder
part: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, Part I — Of Offences Affecting Life
exact_text:
Except in the cases hereinafter excepted, culpable homicide is murder, if the act by which the death is caused is done with the intention of causing death, or—

Secondly.— If it is done with the intention of causing such bodily injury as the offender knows to be likely to cause the death of the person to whom the harm is caused, or—

Thirdly.— If it is done with the intention of causing bodily injury to any person and the bodily injury intended to be inflicted is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, or—

Fourthly.— If the person committing the act knows that it is so imminently dangerous that it must, in all probability, cause death or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, and commits such act without any excuse for incurring the risk of causing death or such injury as aforesaid.
ai_explanation: Section 100 of the BNS 2023 defines 'murder'. Culpable homicide (the unlawful killing of a person) becomes murder when: (1) the act is done with the specific intention to kill; (2) the offender knew the bodily injury they intended would likely cause death; (3) the intended injury is objectively sufficient to cause death; or (4) the act is so imminently dangerous that death is the probable result and no reasonable excuse exists. This provision replaced Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
source_name: Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department, Government of India
version_note: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — in force from 1 July 2024. Replaced IPC s. 300.

short_title: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder
title: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder
part: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, Part I — Of Offences Affecting Life
exact_text:
(1) Whoever commits culpable homicide not amounting to murder shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine, if the act by which death is caused is done with the intention of causing death, or of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death;

(2) or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, or with fine, or with both, if the act is done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause death, but without any intention to cause death, or to cause such bodily injury as is likely to cause death.
ai_explanation: Section 101 of BNS 2023 deals with culpable homicide that does not reach the level of murder. If someone kills another person with the intention of causing death or serious bodily harm likely to cause death, the punishment can be life imprisonment or up to 10 years plus a fine. If the killing was done knowing it was likely to cause death but without an intention to kill, the punishment can be up to 10 years, a fine, or both. This replaced Section 304 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
source_name: Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department, Government of India
version_note: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — in force from 1 July 2024. Replaced IPC s. 304.

title: Punishment for murder
part: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, Part I — Of Offences Affecting Life
exact_text:
(1) Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.

(2) When a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground each member of such group shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.
ai_explanation: Section 103 of BNS 2023 prescribes punishment for the offence of murder. A person convicted of murder may be sentenced to death or life imprisonment, along with a fine. Section 103(2) introduces an important new provision: where a mob of five or more persons commits murder on grounds such as race, caste, community, sex, religion, language, or personal belief, every member of that mob shall be punished with death or life imprisonment plus a fine. This replaced Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
source_name: Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department, Government of India
version_note: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — in force from 1 July 2024. Replaced IPC s. 302.

title: Theft
part: Chapter XVII — Of Offences Against Property
exact_text:
(1) Whoever, intending to take dishonestly any moveable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moves that property in order to such taking, is said to commit theft.

Explanation 1.— A thing so long as it is attached to the earth, not being moveable property, cannot be the subject of theft; but it becomes capable of being the subject of theft as soon as it is severed from the earth.

Explanation 2.— A moving effected by the same act which effects the severance may be a theft.

Explanation 3.— A person is said to cause a thing to move by removing an obstacle which prevented it from moving or by separating it from any other thing, as well as by actually moving it.

Explanation 4.— A person, who by any means causes an animal to move, is said to move that animal, and to move everything which, in consequence of the motion so caused, is moved by that animal.

Explanation 5.— The consent mentioned in the definition may be express or implied, and may be given either by the person in possession, or by any person having for that purpose authority either express or implied.
ai_explanation: Section 303 of BNS 2023 defines the offence of theft. Theft is committed when a person dishonestly takes a moveable property out of someone else's possession without their consent. Key elements: (1) dishonest intention to take; (2) moveable property; (3) from another's possession; (4) without consent; (5) physical movement of the property. Consent may be express or implied. This replaced Section 378 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
source_name: Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department, Government of India
version_note: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — in force from 1 July 2024. Replaced IPC s. 378.

title: Punishment for theft
part: Chapter XVII — Of Offences Against Property
exact_text: Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
ai_explanation: Section 304 of BNS 2023 sets out the punishment for theft. A person convicted of theft may be sentenced to imprisonment (simple or rigorous) for up to three years, or a fine, or both. This replaced Section 379 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
source_name: Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department, Government of India
version_note: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — in force from 1 July 2024. Replaced IPC s. 379.

title: Criminal intimidation
part: Chapter XIX — Of Criminal Intimidation, Insult and Annoyance
exact_text:
(1) Whoever threatens another with any injury to his person, reputation or property, or to the person or reputation of any one in whom that person is interested, with intent to cause alarm to that person, or to cause that person to do any act which he is not legally bound to do, or to omit to do any act which that person is legally entitled to do, as the means of avoiding the execution of such threat, commits criminal intimidation.

Explanation.— A threat to injure the reputation of any deceased person in whom the person threatened is interested, is within this section.
ai_explanation: Section 351 of BNS 2023 defines criminal intimidation. It is committed when a person threatens another with injury to their person, reputation, or property (or that of someone they care about) with the intent to: (a) cause alarm; (b) compel them to do something they are not legally obligated to do; or (c) compel them to refrain from doing something they are legally entitled to do. Threatening the reputation of a deceased person also qualifies. This replaced Section 503 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
source_name: Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department, Government of India
version_note: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — in force from 1 July 2024. Replaced IPC s. 503.

title: Rape
part: Chapter V — Of Offences Against Woman and Child
exact_text:
A man is said to commit "rape" if he—

(a) penetrates his penis, to any extent, into the vagina, mouth, urethra or anus of a woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person; or
(b) inserts, to any extent, any object or a part of the body, not being the penis, into the vagina, the urethra or anus of a woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person; or
(c) manipulates any part of the body of a woman so as to cause penetration into the vagina, urethra, anus or any part of body of such woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person; or
(d) applies his mouth to the vagina, anus, urethra of a woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person,

under the circumstances falling under any of the following seven descriptions:—

Firstly.— Against her will.
Secondly.— Without her consent.
Thirdly.— With her consent, when her consent has been obtained by putting her or any person in whom she is interested, in fear of death or of hurt.
Fourthly.— With her consent, when the man knows that he is not her husband and that her consent is given because she believes that he is another man to whom she is or believes herself to be lawfully married.
Fifthly.— With her consent when, at the time of giving such consent, by reason of unsoundness of mind or intoxication or the administration by him personally or through another of any stupefying or unwholesome substance, she is unable to understand the nature and consequences of that to which she gives consent.
Sixthly.— With or without her consent, when she is under eighteen years of age.
Seventhly.— When she is unable to communicate consent.

Explanation 1.— For the purposes of this section, "vagina" shall also include labia majora.
Explanation 2.— Consent means an unequivocal voluntary agreement when the woman by words, gestures or any form of verbal or non-verbal communication, communicates willingness to participate in the specific sexual act:

Provided that a woman who does not physically resist to the act of penetration shall not by the reason only of that fact, be regarded as consenting to the sexual activity.

Exception 1.— A medical procedure or intervention shall not constitute rape.
Exception 2.— Sexual intercourse or sexual acts by a man with his own wife, the wife not being under eighteen years of age, is not rape.
ai_explanation: Section 63 of BNS 2023 defines the offence of rape. It covers sexual acts committed against a woman without her consent or under circumstances where consent is vitiated (e.g., obtained by force, fear, fraud, intoxication, or unsoundness of mind). Sexual acts with a girl under 18 years of age always constitute rape regardless of consent. The section emphasizes that mere absence of physical resistance does not mean consent. Medical procedures and sexual intercourse within marriage (wife above 18) are excepted. This replaced Section 375 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
source_name: Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department, Government of India
version_note: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — in force from 1 July 2024. Replaced IPC s. 375.

title: Punishment for rape
part: Chapter V — Of Offences Against Woman and Child
exact_text:
(1) Whoever, except in the cases provided for in sub-section (2), commits rape, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than ten years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.

(2) Whoever,—
(a) being a police officer, commits rape—
(i) within the limits of the police station to which such police officer is appointed; or
(ii) in the premises of any station house; or
(iii) on a woman in such police officer's custody or in the custody of a police officer subordinate to such police officer; or
(b) being a public servant, commits rape on a woman in such public servant's custody or in the custody of a public servant subordinate to such public servant; or
(c) being a member of the armed forces deployed in an area by the Central or a State Government commits rape in such area; or
(d) being on the management or on the staff of a jail, remand home or other place of custody established by or under any law for the time being in force or of a women's or children's institution, commits rape on any inmate of such jail, remand home, place or institution; or
(e) being on the management or on the staff of a hospital, commits rape on a woman in that hospital; or
(f) being a relative, guardian or teacher of, or a person in a position of trust or authority towards the woman, commits rape on such woman; or
(g) commits rape during communal or sectarian violence; or
(h) commits rape on a woman knowing her to be pregnant; or
(i) commits rape on a woman incapable of giving consent; or
(j) being in a position of control or dominance over a woman, commits rape on such woman; or
(k) commits rape on a woman suffering from mental or physical disability; or
(l) while committing rape causes grievous bodily harm or maims or disfigures or endangers the life of a woman; or
(m) commits rape repeatedly on the same woman,

shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than ten years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life, which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life, and shall also be liable to fine.
ai_explanation: Section 64 of BNS 2023 prescribes punishment for rape. The minimum punishment is 10 years rigorous imprisonment, extendable to life imprisonment, plus a fine. Enhanced punishment (minimum 10 years up to life meaning natural life) applies in aggravated cases including rape by police officers, public servants, armed forces personnel, hospital staff, persons in positions of authority or trust, during communal violence, on pregnant women, on women with disabilities, or repeated rape of the same victim. This replaced Section 376 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
source_name: Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department, Government of India
version_note: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — in force from 1 July 2024. Replaced IPC s. 376.

title: Definitions
ai_explanation: Section 2 of BNSS 2023 defines key terms used in Indian criminal procedure. Important definitions include: 'bailable offence' (an offence where bail is a right); 'non-bailable offence' (bail is at the court's discretion); 'cognizable offence' (police can arrest without warrant); 'non-cognizable offence' (warrant required for arrest); 'complaint' (allegation to a Magistrate); 'First Information Report' (FIR — the initial police report under Section 173); 'summons-case' and 'warrant-case' (classifications based on offence severity). This replaced Section 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
source_name: Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department, Government of India
version_note: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — in force from 1 July 2024. Replaced CrPC 1973, s. 2.

title: Arrest how made
exact_text:
(1) In making an arrest the police officer or other person making the arrest shall actually touch or confine the body of the person to be arrested, unless there be a submission to the custody by word or action:

Provided that where a woman is to be arrested, unless the circumstances indicate to the contrary, her submission to custody on an oral intimation of arrest shall be presumed and, unless the police officer is a female police officer, the police officer shall not touch the person of the woman for making her arrest.

(2) If such person forcibly resists the endeavour to arrest him, or attempts to evade the arrest, such police officer or other person may use all means necessary to effect the arrest:

Provided that nothing in this sub-section shall be deemed to justify the use of greater restraint than is necessary to prevent the escape of the person arrested.

(3) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to justify the arrest of a person on mere suspicion of an offence.
ai_explanation: Section 35 of BNSS 2023 sets out how arrests are to be made in India. Physical contact or confinement is required unless the person submits voluntarily. When arresting a woman, submission to oral intimation of arrest is presumed, and male officers should not touch a woman during arrest. Reasonable force may be used if the person resists, but no more force than necessary is permitted. A person cannot be arrested on mere suspicion alone. This replaced Section 46 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
source_name: Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department, Government of India
version_note: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — in force from 1 July 2024. Replaced CrPC 1973, s. 46.

short_title: Information in cognizable cases — First Information Report
title: Information in cognizable cases
part: Chapter XII — Information to the Police and Their Powers to Investigate
exact_text:
(1) Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence, irrespective of the area where the offence is committed, may be given orally or in writing, to an officer in charge of a police station and if given orally, shall be reduced to writing by him or under his direction, and be read over to the informant; and every such information, whether given in writing or reduced to writing as aforesaid, shall be signed by the person giving it, and the substance thereof shall be entered in such form as the State Government may prescribe by rules in this behalf, in a book to be kept by such officer in such form as the State Government may prescribe in this behalf:

Provided that if the information is given by the woman against whom an offence under section 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 69, 70, 71, 74, 76, 77, 78, 79 or 124 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is alleged to have been committed or attempted, then such information shall be recorded, by a female police officer or any police officer:

Provided further that where the person giving such information is temporarily or permanently mentally or physically disabled, it shall be recorded by a police officer, at the residence of the person seeking to report such offence or at a convenient place of such person's choice, in the presence of an interpreter or a special educator, as the case may be:

(2) A copy of the information as recorded under sub-section (1) shall be given forthwith, free of cost, to the informant.

(3) Any person aggrieved by a refusal on the part of an officer in charge of a police station to record the information referred to in sub-section (1) may send the substance of such information, in writing and by post, to the Superintendent of Police concerned who, if satisfied that such information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence, shall either investigate the case himself or direct an investigation to be made by any police officer subordinate to him.
ai_explanation: Section 173 of BNSS 2023 governs the First Information Report (FIR) — the formal police document recording an initial complaint about a cognizable offence. Key rights for citizens: (1) An FIR can be filed at any police station regardless of where the offence occurred (Zero FIR); (2) A free copy of the FIR must be given to the informant; (3) If police refuse to register an FIR, the complainant can write to the Superintendent of Police; (4) Women reporting sexual offences must have their FIR recorded by a female officer where possible; (5) Disabled persons can have their FIR recorded at a place convenient to them. This replaced Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
source_name: Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department, Government of India
version_note: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — in force from 1 July 2024. Replaced CrPC 1973, s. 154.

title: Maximum period for which an undertrial prisoner can be detained
part: Chapter XXXV — Bail and Bail Bonds
exact_text:
(1) Where a person has been in detention as an undertrial prisoner for a period extending to one-half of the maximum period of imprisonment specified for that offence under the law, he shall be released on bail:

Provided that the Court, after recording its reasons in writing, may refuse bail in such cases of—
(a) offences where the punishment is death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term of ten years or more;
(b) cases involving offences where investigation has not been completed within the aforesaid period;
(c) cases involving offences where the person has been previously convicted for the offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term of ten years or more.

(2) No person shall be detained in custody after the expiry of one-third of the maximum period of imprisonment specified for that offence if he is a first-time offender.

(3) The provisions of sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) shall not apply to any person who is accused of an offence under any law other than this Sanhita.
ai_explanation: Section 479 of BNSS 2023 is an important right for undertrial prisoners (persons imprisoned while awaiting trial). If you have been detained as an undertrial for half the maximum sentence for the alleged offence, you are entitled to bail. First-time offenders are entitled to bail after serving one-third of the maximum sentence. Courts may refuse bail in serious cases (offences carrying death, life imprisonment, or 10+ years) or where investigation is incomplete. This provision aims to prevent excessive pre-trial detention. It replaced Section 436A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
source_name: Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department, Government of India
version_note: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — in force from 1 July 2024. Replaced CrPC 1973, s. 436A.

title: Definitions
ai_explanation: Section 2 of BSA 2023 defines core terms of Indian evidence law. Key definitions: 'evidence' includes oral testimony of witnesses and documentary evidence (including electronic/digital records). 'Document' now explicitly includes electronic and digital records. 'Fact' means anything perceivable by senses or any mental condition. 'Proved' means the court believes a fact exists or finds its existence highly probable. 'Disproved' means the court finds the fact unlikely to exist. 'Not proved' is the middle ground — neither proved nor disproved. These definitions replaced Section 3 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
source_name: Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department, Government of India
version_note: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 — in force from 1 July 2024. Replaced Indian Evidence Act 1872, s. 3.

title: Oral evidence
part: Part II — Of the Relevancy of Facts, Chapter V — Of Documentary Evidence
exact_text: All facts, except the contents of documents or electronic records, may be proved by oral evidence.
ai_explanation: Section 57 of BSA 2023 establishes the general rule that facts may be proved through oral testimony in court, subject to the exception that the contents of documents (including electronic records) must be proved through the document itself, not by oral evidence. This maintains the original evidence rule that documentary content requires documentary proof. It replaced Section 59 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
source_name: Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department, Government of India
version_note: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 — in force from 1 July 2024. Replaced Indian Evidence Act 1872, s. 59.

title: Admissibility of electronic records
part: Part II — Of the Relevancy of Facts, Chapter V — Of Documentary Evidence
ai_explanation: Section 65 of BSA 2023 governs the admissibility of electronic records as evidence in court. Electronic records — including emails, digital documents, printouts, data stored in computer systems, or transmitted over networks — are admissible as documentary evidence if four conditions are met: (1) the computer was used to regularly store or process information in normal business activities; (2) the type of information in the electronic record was regularly fed into the computer in ordinary course; (3) the computer was operating properly for most of the relevant period; (4) the electronic record reproduces information fed into the computer during normal activities. This is a significant provision for digital evidence in cybercrime cases. It expanded and replaced Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
source_name: Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department, Government of India
version_note: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 — in force from 1 July 2024. Replaced Indian Evidence Act 1872, s. 65B.

title: Burden of proof
part: Part III — Production and Effect of Evidence, Chapter X — Of the Burden of Proof
exact_text:
Whoever desires any Court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts, must prove that those facts exist.

When a person is bound to prove the existence of any fact, it is said that the burden of proof lies on that person.
ai_explanation: Section 111 of BSA 2023 establishes the fundamental rule of burden of proof. In any legal proceeding, the person who asserts the existence of a fact and seeks a legal remedy based on it bears the burden of proving that fact. This means a person filing a suit or pressing a criminal case must provide evidence to establish their claims. This foundational rule is the cornerstone of adversarial legal proceedings and replaced Section 101 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
source_name: Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department, Government of India
version_note: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 — in force from 1 July 2024. Replaced Indian Evidence Act 1872, s. 101.
